Hi Lena — thanks for the clear questions. Short answer up front: we try to bill in a way that follows active context affinity within a 15-minute interaction window by default, but there are important caveats for long summarization bursts that cross model token thresholds. Below is an example and then a proposed compromise for Acme’s SOW.

Example (default platform behavior):
- Call A (streaming): 200 tokens generated at 08:00, prefix warmed for user session.
- Call B (long): 8,000 tokens generated at 08:03.
- Because Call B is within the 15-minute interaction window and reuses the session prefix, we attribute Call A to the same billable session and the billing quantum is applied to the combined session tokens (8,200) — no separate minimum for the 200-token call.

Rounding and floors:
- Per-token meter units are recorded at generation time, then line-itemized on the invoice after applying three rules in order: 1) quantum floor (default 100-token floor for microcalls), 2) aggregation (session-level rollup within the interaction window), 3) invoice rounding (round to nearest whole billing unit).

Known caveat: very long calls (>16k tokens) are chunked at model-compatibility boundaries and may introduce additional per-chunk minimums if they span multiple serving slices.

Proposed SOW compromise for Acme:
- Interaction window: 15 minutes (default)
- Microcall floor: 100 tokens (applies when a session only contains microcalls and never crosses 1,000 tokens within the window)
- Long-call exemption: if any single call in the window >2,048 tokens (configurable per-customer), microcall floors in the same window are ignored and full session token sum is billed (no double-flooring).

I’m attaching a short workbook with sample math. Happy to run a couple of Acme-specific invoices against this logic.

Hi Lena — adding the billing formatting you asked for. Below is a short invoice-style example pulled from the attached workbook. Numbers are illustrative.

Invoice example (windowed attribution):
- Session window: 08:00 - 08:15
  - Microcall at 08:00: 200 tokens generated (prefix reused)
  - Long call at 08:03: 8,000 tokens generated
  - Session total: 8,200 tokens
  - Metering: No microfloor applied (because session crosses long-call threshold per Markus’ proposed rule)
  - Billable units: 8,200 tokens (rounded → 8,200)

Alternate case (microcalls only):
- Session window: 10:00 - 10:12
  - 3 microcalls: 120, 90, 80 tokens (separate short requests but same session)
  - Raw total: 290 tokens
  - Microfloor rule: apply 100-token floor per session? We apply single session floor → max(290,100) = 290 (no extra inflation).

Notes: the key difference that trips customers up is whether the platform treats the small call as an independent billed unit (microfloor × N) or lumps it into the session total.  Default is the latter.

Hi Lena — quick answers to your two asks and an additional operational note.

1) Tenant-level config & reconciliation fields: yes, the interaction window is configurable (default 15m). We will add a session_id and window_id to the billing export for Acme so your finance team can reconcile line-by-line. We’ll include a mapping column 'window_trigger' that flags whether the microfloor was suppressed because of a long-call exemption.

2) Rounding rule: we round to the nearest whole billing unit after aggregation. For tokenization we bill integer tokens; fractional tokens (post-compression or sampling heuristics) are summed then rounded to nearest integer. Example: 8,200.6 → invoice shows 8,201 tokens. If you prefer a conservative round-down policy for the pilot period, we can make that a contract term for the first 90 days.

Operational note: to avoid surprises, we recommend enabling 'session sticky routing' for your production tenant so prefix reuse is more predictable across quickly-interleaved calls.

Proposed concession: 5% off list for first 90 days and pilot-friendly round-down invoice rule (8,200.6 → 8,200) if contract signed by Oct 15.

If that works, I’ll produce a one-page amendment and a sample invoice showing the round-down vs round-to-nearest.
